question: Can a Muslim take part in a workplace gift exchange held around Christmas?
asked: In my workplace there is a gift exchange around this time. Even though the word Christmas is not mentioned, it happens in this season, and everybody puts an anonymous gift into a pool. If I don't participate it looks very bad, and if I do, am I committing any sin?
answer:
So this is now the corporate setting. We are now talking about you in your office place, and you have these various things taking place in your office. Once again, we need to look at what is going on with this gift exchange. Is there any hint of worshipping other than Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala? Are people giving their servitude to another god in this corporate environment? Or is it being done for camaraderie, for a pleasant environment in the corporation?

I think it is very clear, given the circumstances that we live in now, given especially the secular nature of the Western world, that these gifts are not being done to worship other than Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala. You are not presenting it to a god, a false god. You're not presenting a platter to an idol. This is a mutual gift exchange that is done for camaraderie, for building some office rapport.

And in fact, we have authentic narrations from the Sahabah in this regard, of accepting gifts. In fact, the riwayat I'm going to report to you are much more than what this brother is asking about. This brother is asking about secular, corporate, generic festivals in the America that we live in. This is not in the church. The Sahabah, the athar I'm quoting you, they were gifted by the religious communities because of the religious festival, not just some generic stuff.

And realize that the Sahabah conquered lands that were majority non-Muslim. In particular Iraq, and of course Syria, but Iraq when they conquered it was a land that was predominantly Zoroastrian. They were what we now call in our lands Parsis. We call them, in our India, Pakistan, Parsis. They were called Parsis because they came from Persia. These Zoroastrians came to India because the Muslims conquered. So these Zoroastrians were the predominant people of those regions, and there are multiple narrations from the Sahabah regarding the gifts that happened on their festival days, the festival day of Nauruz, for example.

So of them, for example, 'Ali radiyallahu 'anhu, when he was the Khalifah of Kufa, and of course he was surrounded by Zoroastrians: on the day of Nauruz he was gifted with many gifts from their religious leaders, from the people. He's the leader now, and these are minorities, so they want to give. So he was gifted many gifts, and he accepted all of them. No problem.

Another narration, I love this narration, you'll see why. He was gifted something called faludaj. This is in the hadith, by the way. Desi people, faludaj isn't Pakistani, don't worry. It goes back to ancient Faris, ancient Persia. You did not invent faludaj, don't worry. It goes back, but the term is exactly the same. Now, their faludaj wasn't mango and kulfi and ice cream. Their faludaj was honey and milk and other things. Of course, we now have version 3275, I think, but their asl faludaj was a cold drink of milk and honey and other things. Now we have added mango lassi and other things, and the weird, weird worms... what do you call it? Spaghetti noodles that are there, all of that. I'm pretty sure the ancient Iranians did not have that. Oh Arabs, you don't have faludaj, right? You have no idea what faludaj is. You don't know what you're missing.

So 'Ali radiyallahu 'anhu, and you will see why I love this narration, and my respect for 'Ali radiyallahu 'anhu went up ten notches after this narration when I first came across it: 'Ali radiyallahu 'anhu was gifted faludaj. He ate it, and he loved it. MashaAllah, man after my heart. He said, "What is this?" They said, "It is faludaj." He said, "What's this? Why are you gifting? What is going on?" So they said, "Today is Nauruz." Nauruz, of course, by the way, what is Nauruz? Naya roz, still in our Sanskrit: new day. Today is Nauruz, the festival of the new year, the holy day, the holiest day for the Zoroastrians. And still to this day, Iran celebrates Nauruz; even the Muslim population celebrates Nauruz. It has become a different thing, but anyway, back then it was a religious festival, akin to Christmas or Hanukkah or whatever.

Today is the day of Nauruz. Nauruz is a religious festival. They gifted 'Ali radiyallahu 'anhu faludaj. What did my man say when he was gifted faludaj? "May every day be a Nauruz for you." He went up in respect. Anyway, that was just a joke; he is deserving of our respect whether we like faludaj or not. But if you like faludaj, then mashaAllah.

But here's the point, and subhanAllah, and again, to be gentle: some strands interpret Islam in a manner that life becomes so difficult and unreasonable, and they claim to follow the salaf, and the salaf themselves had very different lives from those who claim to follow them in our times. 'Ali radiyallahu 'anhu: who is he? I mean, do I need to give you the fada'il of 'Ali? Is anybody going to accuse him of not following the salaf enough? He is the salaf. 'Ali radiyallahu 'anhu is being gifted faludaj on the day of Nauruz. Like, imagine a Christian gifting you: "Because it is Christmas, I'm gifting you this." And he smirks, he smiles, he goes, "Great, every day should be Nauruz. Give me this every day, I don't mind." You are not worshipping other than Allah when you eat faludaj on Nauruz, alhamdulillah for that. You're not worshipping other than Allah if your Christian neighbor gives you something on Christmas. He's being happy on his day; he gives you something.

Now, there are some conditions, and I'll mention them. 'A'ishah radiyallahu 'anha was asked by one of the Sahabah. So some of the Sahabah are back in Madinah now; 'A'ishah never went over there to live. Somebody is in Madinah and she asks 'A'ishah, "We have some Zoroastrian neighbors. They gift us fi 'idihim, which is their Nauruz. What do we do? Can we accept or not?" What does our mother say, radiyallahu 'anha? "Listen: whatever was sacrificed on that day, do not eat. But whatever comes to you from fruits and plants," meaning vegetables and non-meat, "eat."

So on that day they're going to sacrifice to the false gods; they're going to mention the name of other than Allah 'azza wa jall. Don't eat that meat. Zoroastrians, because Zoroastrian meat is different than Ahl al-Kitab. You should know this: Zoroastrian meat is not Ahl al-Kitab. So the meat, don't eat. But the fruits and vegetables, and faludaj is basically non-meat, alhamdulillah, she said eat from it. The sweets, eat from it, no problem. This is 'A'ishah.

As well, we have Abu Barzah, who settled also in Iraq, and he would tell his family, his wife and his children, that on the day of Nauruz, anything that comes to you from the meat, don't eat, but anything else that comes, go ahead and accept it and eat from it. So what was haram was their sacrifice, because the Zoroastrians are not Ahl al-Kitab. So if they give you some meat, do not take their meat. But if they give you anything else, sweets, halwa, laddu, anything, no problem, accept it. These are the Sahabah, and their day was the holy day.

So in the corporate world that we live in, this isn't even Christmas, what they're asking us to do. There is no deification done. Nobody is worshipping a baby god. Nothing like this is happening. It's just a generic... Now obviously, if we're in a Muslim land and you are a corporate owner, why would you do this on the 25th of December? For you I will say, fear Allah 'azza wa jall; we have our rituals, we have our festival. But when you are going to work and the corporation over here has announced, "Okay, on the..." When is it usually done, before Christmas or after Christmas? Before Christmas, the 20th or so, right, in the week before? "On the 15th, whatever, on this day everybody bring a $20 gift; we'll pull our names from a bag and we'll just swap over gifts." Okay, where is the worship being done to other than Allah? Nothing. How can it be made haram? I agree, if you are in charge of the company and you're in a Muslim land, why would you bring in the 25th of December? But that's not the case here.

So **there is nothing wrong whatsoever in participating in this exchange of gifts.** In fact, even more than this: if they actually gift you on the day, for the day, because of the day, we have the athar of the Sahabah here. You can accept, and then when your turn comes, you gift them back. When it's the day of Eid, I actually encourage all of you on the day of Eid to bring something special for your colleagues, to bring something extra. This is a means of da'wah. Nobody can say no to some baklava. Nobody can say no to some nice gulab jamun, or bring faludaj, mashaAllah, because we have adopted faludaj now. We took it from them, we upped the bar, we raised it, mashaAllah, because now faludaj has the mother of all, which is ice cream. Ben and Jerry's vanilla, by the way, works well on faludaj, just FYI. So if you gift your colleagues faludaj, it's going to be a bit difficult, but if you manage to do that, or anything good on the day of Eid, and then they gift you back on their Christmas or holy days, there's nothing wrong with this, as long as what they're gifting you is halal, obviously.
